```{r setup, include = FALSE, echo = FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# ---------------- Table Theme -----------------
tbl_size <- 12  # the brief asks for Arial 12 throughout; reduce only if a wide table cannot fit

themed_table <- function(df, caption = NULL, align = NULL, size = tbl_size) {
  ft <- flextable(df)
  ft <- font(ft, fontname = "Arial", part = "all")
  ft <- fontsize(ft, size = size, part = "all")
  ft <- bg(ft, bg = map_high, part = "header")
  ft <- color(ft, color = "white", part = "header")
  ft <- bold(ft, part = "header")
  if (nrow(df) >= 2) ft <- bg(ft, i = seq(2, nrow(df), by = 2), bg = map_low, part = "body")
  ft <- border_remove(ft)
  ft <- hline(ft, border = officer::fp_border(color = map_na, width = 1), part = "body")
  ft <- hline_bottom(ft, border = officer::fp_border(color = blue_dark, width = 1.5), part = "body")
  if (!is.null(align)) {                      # e.g. "llr" = left, left, right
    al <- c(l = "left", c = "center", r = "right")[strsplit(align, "")[[1]]]
    for (k in seq_along(al)) ft <- align(ft, j = k, align = unname(al[k]), part = "all")
  }
  if (!is.null(caption)) ft <- set_caption(ft, caption = caption)
  autofit(ft)
}

```

## Chapter 4: Findings

This chapter builds on the empirical research documented in the methodology chapter. It presents the results of the various analyses, building up to the creation of the decision framework aiding model selection.

### Predictive Performance Results

The study ranks the predictive performance of the model classes as GBM, then ANN, then GLM. The sensitivity models are included to test whether the configuration choice significantly affects predictive performance of the respective models. However, they follow the same trend, with the GBM sensitivity model scoring 0.2427 and the ANN sensitivity scoring 0.2454 on deviance. This means that the configuration choice does not affect the ranking of the model classes.

```{r tab-test-performance, echo=FALSE}
te <- ev$metrics[ev$metrics$set == "test", ]
themed_table(
  data.frame(Model              = lab(te$model),
             Deviance           = fmt(te$deviance),
             `Log-likelihood`   = fmt(te$loglik),
             `Gini Coefficient` = fmt(te$gini, 4),
             Calibration        = fmt(te$calibration, 4),
             check.names = FALSE),
  align = "lrrrr", 
  caption = paste("Test-set performance")
)
```

From 3,000 bootstrap resamples of covariate-profile groups in the test dataset, the investigation builds the table below to summarise this comparison. The selected GBM outperforms the GLM by 2.6% given by the 0.0064 difference in deviance on a 95% confidence interval where the two have a deviance of 0.0037 to 0.0108. Similarly, the selected ANN improves on the GLM by 1.1% and the selected GBM improves on the ANN by 1.4%. During tuning, the cross-validated loss shows changes that guide the selection of the optimal hyperparameter configuration. However, the tuning surfaces are flat for both boosting machines and neural networks. Therefore, the choice of configuration does not make a practical difference in the accuracy of the model. Similarly, ranking is preserved by the sensitivity configurations, meaning that the simplicity rule applied does not affect predictive accuracy on held-out data.

```{r fig-paired-differences-in-test-deviance}
# ---- Paired differences in test deviance (forest plot) ------------
d1 <- ev$diff_table
d1$comparison <- paste(model_labels[d1$first], "vs", model_labels[d1$second])

# table order, top to bottom
d1$comparison <- factor(d1$comparison, levels = rev(d1$comparison))

fig1 <- ggplot(d1, aes(x = diff, y = comparison)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi)) +
  labs(x = "Difference in mean test deviance (negative: first model better)", 
       y = NULL) + base_theme
fig1
```

The study also reviews the train-test gap in accuracy, which defines overfitting in the study. The deviance gap, as illustrated in the table below, is larger in more flexible models. The gap ranges between 0.0075 and 0.0113 across all five models. This gap indicates minimal overfitting as the GLM is completely deterministic. Measuring against it as a benchmark, the models show an even narrower gap, 0.002 and 0.004 for the GBM and 0.001 for both ANNs. Gini index shows a similar trend, albeit with a much smaller gap between train and test runs.

```{r tab-train-test, echo=FALSE}
m  <- ev$metrics
tr <- m[m$set == "train", ]
te <- m[m$set == "test", ]
te <- te[match(tr$model, te$model), ]
themed_table(
  data.frame(Model             = lab(tr$model),
             `Train deviance`  = fmt(tr$deviance),
             `Test deviance`   = fmt(te$deviance),
             `Deviance gap`    = fmt(te$deviance - tr$deviance),
             `Train Gini`      = fmt(tr$gini, 3),
             `Test Gini`       = fmt(te$gini, 3),
             `Gini gap`        = fmt(tr$gini - te$gini, 3),
             check.names = FALSE),
  align = "lrrrrrr", 
  caption = "Training and Test Performance Gaps"
)
```

### Explainability

#### Explanation Fidelity Results

Fidelity examines how accurate a model's feature attributions are as a description of its behaviour. The efficiency check tests the gap between the sum of a policy's SHAP attributions and its prediction, less the baseline, in log frequency units, and returns the maximum efficiency error for each model class which is consistently under the 1e-8 threshold.

```{r tab-efficiency, echo=FALSE}
eff <- shp$efficiency_error   # largest error per model, from the full run
themed_table(
  data.frame(Model = as.character(lab(names(eff))),
             `Max efficiency error` = format(eff, scientific = TRUE, digits = 3),
             Threshold = "1e-8",
             Pass = ifelse(eff < 1e-8, "Yes", "No"),
             check.names = FALSE),
  caption = paste("Efficiency Check"),
  align = "lrrc")
```

Fidelity is measured through the faithfulness correlation. Since a GLM is additive on the log scale, removing a set of features from the dataset reduces the contribution by the sum of the attributions of the missing features. Its faithfulness correlation is 1 and the RMSE is near-zero. With this definition,the GLM's fidelity serves as a reliable benchmark to help one understand fidelity in other models. The fidelity of selected GBM and ANN models have a SHAP fidelity correlation of 0.974 and 0.973 respectively. Their sensitivity versions show a correlation of 0.970 and 0.972. SHAP faithfulness RMSE quantifies the error demonstrated by determining the root mean squared gap between SHAP's predicted drop in the prediction and the actual deviation that occurs when the model is ran and explained. As shown below, the RMSE, which is reported in log units, ranges between 0.067 and 0.079. This represents an error ranging between 7% and 8%.

```{r tab-shap-fidelity-summary, echo=FALSE}
fidelity <- shp$shap_faith_summary

themed_table(
  data.frame(
    Model = lab(fidelity$model),
    `Mean fidelity correlation` = fmt(fidelity$faith_cor, 3),
    `Correlation standard error` = fmt(fidelity$faith_cor_se, 3),
    `Mean RMSE` = fmt(fidelity$faith_rmse, 4),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  align = "lrrr",
  
  caption = paste("SHAP fidelity averaged across explained test policies"
  )
)
```

The correlations above do not effectively distinguish the fidelity between the models, as their variations are within noise. This is especially true given the standard error ranging at about 0.0015. However, there is a distinctive drop in the correlation for the sensitivity models which are more complex than the selected ones. There is also a trend where all the 5 models show a slightly reduced fidelity in the middle deciles, dropping to around 0.96. This is better illustrated in the figure below.

```{r tab-shap-fidelity-by-risk-band, echo=FALSE}
fd <- as.data.frame(as.table(as.matrix(shp$shap_faith_decile)))
names(fd) <- c("decile", "model", "faith_cor")
fd$decile <- as.integer(as.character(fd$decile)); fd$lab <- lab(fd$model)
fidelity_by_risk_band <- ggplot(fd, aes(x = decile, 
                                        y = faith_cor, 
                                        olour = lab, 
                                        shape = lab, 
                                        linetype = lab, 
                                        group = lab)) +
  geom_line() + geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10) + scale_model() +
  labs(x = "Predicted-risk decile (1 = lowest)", y = "SHAP faithfulness (correlation)") +
  base_theme
fidelity_by_risk_band
```

Fidelity is also examined for LIME. The variation of the surrogate $R^2$ between the 5 models is shown below. While the GLM retains the highest correlation, it has a faithfulness lower than 1 because unlike with SHAP, its weights are coefficients of the surrogate model rather than exact contributions. The LIME surrogate's fit, faithfulness, and stability are summarised in the table below, by binning scheme and model.

```{r tab-lime-metrics, echo=FALSE}
lime <- lm_$lime_summary
scheme_labels <- c(
  prespecified_bins = "Prespecified bins",
  default_lime_bins = "LIME default bins",
  no_bins = "No binning"
)

themed_table(
  data.frame(
    Scheme = unname(scheme_labels[as.character(lime$scheme)]),
    Model = lab(lime$model),
    `Surrogate R-squared` = fmt(lime$lime_r2, 3),
    `Faithfulness correlation` = ifelse(
      is.na(lime$lime_faith_cor), "Not assessed", fmt(lime$lime_faith_cor, 3)
    ),
    `Global importance rank correlation` = fmt(lime$global_rank_cor, 3),
    `Top-three overlap` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * lime$top3_overlap),
    `Local rank correlation` = fmt(lime$local_rank_cor, 3),
    `Relative attribution SD` = fmt(lime$rel_sd, 3),
    `Sign agreement` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * lime$sign_agreement),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  align = "llrrrrrrr",
  
  caption = paste(
    "LIME Surrogate Fit, Faithfulness, and Stability"
  )
)
```

As shown in the trends above, the explanation fidelity falls from 1 to 0.97 in the first step down from the GLM. After this initial drop, the correlation remains flat with variations in the predictive performance. This suggests that non-additivity has the highest impact on explanation fidelity. This suggests that predictive performance and explanation fidelity do not exhibit monotonic co-variation. The figure below illustrates this relationship succinctly, plotting fidelity against performance.

```{r tab-rq1-performance-and-fidelity, echo=FALSE}
d2 <- merge(ev$single_ci[, c("model", "deviance", "dev_lo", "dev_hi")],
            shp$shap_faith_summary[, c("model", "faith_cor", "faith_cor_se")], by = "model")
d2$lab    <- lab(d2$model)
d2$fid_lo <- d2$faith_cor - 1.96 * d2$faith_cor_se
d2$fid_hi <- pmin(1, d2$faith_cor + 1.96 * d2$faith_cor_se)
pvf <- ggplot(d2, aes(x = deviance, y = faith_cor, colour = lab, shape = lab)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = fid_lo, ymax = fid_hi), alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = dev_lo, xmax = dev_hi), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = lab), vjust = -1.2, size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_x_reverse() +
  scale_model() +
  labs(x = "Mean test deviance (reversed: better to the right)",
       y = "SHAP faithfulness (correlation)") +
  base_theme + theme(legend.position = "none")
pvf
```

The pattern indicated in the figure is elaborated in the table below, illustrating the meagre gains in explanation fidelity with increase in predictive performance. The LIME results use the prespecified binning approach.

#### Explanation Stability Results

The standard deviation of attribution ranges from 0.0195 to 0.0222 log units, evening out to about 2% for every model. The local rank correlation is the lowest for the GLM at 0.873, and highest for the selected GBM at 0.914. Sign agreement shows a different order from the other metrics, ranging from 0.966 for the ANN sensitivity model to 0.983 for the GLM. These metrics summarise the explainer-noise floor as shown below:

```{r tab-noise-floor, echo=FALSE}
f1 <- stab$stab_axis1   # axis 1: same fitted model, repeated background samples
themed_table(
  data.frame(Model                          = as.character(lab(f1$model)),
             `SD of attribution (log units)` = sprintf("%.4f", f1$mean_sd_phi),
             `Premium-equivalent (%)`        = sprintf("%.1f", 100 * f1$premium_equiv),
             `Local rank correlation`        = sprintf("%.3f", f1$local_rank_cor),
             `Sign agreement`                = sprintf("%.3f", f1$sign_agreement),
             check.names = FALSE),
  caption = sprintf(paste("Explainer-noise floor: each fitted model explained %d times with different",
                          "50-row background samples, for the same 100 policies (SHAP). The floor",
                          "depends on the background size."), f1$R[1]),
  align = "lrrrr")
```

The table below shows the variation of variables in `shap_metrics()` across the 3 model classes refitted on grouped bootstrap samples.

```{r tab-shap-stability-under-refits, echo=FALSE}
stability <- lm_$rq3

themed_table(
  data.frame(
    Model = lab(stability$model),
    Refits = stability$R,
    `Global rank correlation` = fmt(stability$global_rank_cor, 3),
    `Top-three overlap` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * stability$top3_overlap),
    `Local rank correlation` = fmt(stability$local_rank_cor, 3),
    `Attribution profile distance` = fmt(stability$profile_tv, 3),
    `Mean attribution SD (log scale)` = fmt(stability$mean_sd_phi, 4),
    `Premium-equivalent SD` = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * stability$premium_equiv),
    `Relative attribution SD` = fmt(stability$rel_sd, 3),
    `Sign agreement` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * stability$sign_agreement),
    `Mean prediction SD (log scale)` = fmt(stability$pred_sd, 4),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  align = "lr",
  
  caption = "SHAP Stability Metrics"
)
```

Although it uses the same binning techniques as SHAP, the LIME stability calculation uses a different sampling protocol, with 10 repeats on the same 60 policies with different random perturbations. The GLM has the lowest relative standard deviation but the highest sign agreement under the 3 binning approaches. As illustrated below, the ordering of the three model classes changes with the binning scheme. The global rank correlation and the top 3 overlap for all the models lie near the ceiling, ranging between 0.98 and 1.

```{r tab-lime-stability, echo=FALSE}
scheme_labels <- c(prespecified_bins = "Fixed bins (primary)", C = "Fixed bins (primary)",
                   default_lime_bins = "Default bins",         A = "Default bins",
                   no_bins = "No binning",                     D = "No binning")
ls_ <- lm_$lime_summary
sl  <- unname(scheme_labels[as.character(ls_$scheme)])
sl[is.na(sl)] <- as.character(ls_$scheme)[is.na(sl)]
ls_$scheme_lab <- factor(sl, levels = c("Fixed bins (primary)", "Default bins", "No binning"))
ls_ <- ls_[order(ls_$scheme_lab, as.integer(lab(ls_$model))), ]

themed_table(
  data.frame(Scheme                    = ifelse(duplicated(ls_$scheme_lab), "", as.character(ls_$scheme_lab)),
             Model                     = as.character(lab(ls_$model)),
             `Relative SD`             = sprintf("%.3f", ls_$rel_sd),
             `Sign agreement`          = sprintf("%.3f", ls_$sign_agreement),
             `Local rank correlation`  = sprintf("%.3f", ls_$local_rank_cor),
             `Global rank correlation` = sprintf("%.3f", ls_$global_rank_cor),
             `Top-3 overlap`           = sprintf("%.3f", ls_$top3_overlap),
             check.names = FALSE),
  caption = sprintf(paste("LIME explainer-noise stability")),
  align = "llrrrrr"
  )
```

For both SHAP and LIME, explanation instability increases with model flexibility. For ANN and GBM, this instability exceeds the explainer-noise floor established by the instability of GLMs. It is largely inherited from prediction instability, and demonstrates reallocation ranging between 1.4 to 1.8 times the explainer-noise while the GLM does not exceed it. The complete results are described in much more detail in the appendix and the study's repository on Github.

### Decision Matrix

The evidence matrix below forms the basis for the decision framework. It reports measures of the accuracy, explainability, and robustness aspects of the 5 models tested. The triangles in table headers indicate the direction of better models with regard to that measure. For instance, models with lower deviance are better, so deviance is marked with $▿$.

```{r tab-evidence-matrix, echo=FALSE}
te <- ev$metrics[ev$metrics$set == "test", c("model", "deviance", 
                                             "gini", "calibration")]
fi <- shp$shap_faith_summary[, c("model", "faith_cor", "faith_rmse")]
st <- stab$stab_axis2[, c("model", "premium_equiv", 
                          "sign_agreement", "profile_tv")]

evidence_matrix <- Reduce(function(a, b) merge(a, b, by = "model", all.x = TRUE), 
                          list(te, fi, st))
evidence_matrix <- evidence_matrix[match(names(model_labels), 
                                         evidence_matrix$model), ]
f  <- function(x, d) ifelse(is.na(x), "–", formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d))

themed_table(
  data.frame(Model                       = as.character(lab(evidence_matrix$model)),
             `Deviance ▿`                = f(evidence_matrix$deviance, 4),
             `Gini ▵`                    = f(evidence_matrix$gini, 3),
             `SHAP fidelity ▿`           = f(evidence_matrix$faith_rmse, 4),
             `Refit SD, premium % ▿`     = f(100 * evidence_matrix$premium_equiv, 1),
             `Sign agreement ▵`          = f(evidence_matrix$sign_agreement, 3),
             `Profile distance ▿`        = f(evidence_matrix$profile_tv, 3),
             check.names = FALSE),
  caption = paste("Evidence Matrix: Test-Set Performance, SHAP Fidelity, and Refit Stability"),
  align = "lrrrrrr")
```

The study considers three scenarios to determine the weights.

- Accuracy led pricing - Aiming for the most competitive pricing
- Governance led pricing - Aiming for the most transparent and stable prices
- Balanced pricing - Aiming for a balance between transparency and competitive pricing

The above approaches are actualized in the matrix by the proportional weights assigned to the respective measures. The matrix for the accuracy led pricing approach takes shape by assigning a weight 60 points for performance, with a disproportionately high weight assigned to Gini than to test deviance. It assigns equal points for refit SD, sign agreement, and profile distance to make 20 robustness points, and 20 points for SHAP fidelity through the fidelity RMSE. The resulting ranking is shown below:

```{r decision-framework-rubric, echo=FALSE}
# -------------------------- 1. The rubric ----------------------------
criteria <- data.frame(
  criterion       = c("Deviance", "Gini", 
                      "Refit SD (premium %)", "Sign agreement",
                      "Profile distance", "Fidelity RMSE (log units)"),
  
  column          = c("deviance", "gini", 
                      "refit_sd_pct", "sign_agreement",
                      "profile_tv", "faith_rmse"),
  
  pillar          = c("Performance", "Performance", 
                      "Robustness", "Robustness",
                      "Robustness", "Explainability"),
  # deviance is the primary scoring rule
  share_in_pillar = c(0.60, 0.40, 1/3, 1/3, 1/3, 1),
  # sign agreement cannot fall below 0.5 
  worst           = c(0.2550, 0.200, 5.0, 0.5, 0.25, 0.10),   
  best            = c(0.2400, 0.350, 0.0, 1.0, 0.00, 0.00),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
stopifnot(all(abs(tapply(criteria$share_in_pillar, 
                         criteria$pillar, sum) - 1) < 1e-9))

# ------------------------- 2. Candidate models -----------------------------
models_with_stability <- evidence_matrix[!is.na(evidence_matrix$premium_equiv), ]
models_with_stability$refit_sd_pct <- 100 * models_with_stability$premium_equiv
model_names <- as.character(lab(models_with_stability$model))

score_criterion <- function(value, worst, best) {
  pmin(pmax((value - worst) / (best - worst), 0), 1)
}
criterion_scores <- sapply(seq_len(nrow(criteria)), function(i)
  score_criterion(models_with_stability[[criteria$column[i]]], 
                  criteria$worst[i], criteria$best[i]))
colnames(criterion_scores) <- criteria$criterion
rownames(criterion_scores) <- models_with_stability$model

pillars <- unique(criteria$pillar)

# each pillar on a 0-1 scale
pillar_scores_01 <- sapply(pillars, function(p) {
  k <- criteria$pillar == p
  as.numeric(criterion_scores[, k, drop = FALSE] %*% criteria$share_in_pillar[k])
})
rownames(pillar_scores_01) <- rownames(criterion_scores)

# ------------------- 3. Points for a set of pillar weights -------------------
compute_points <- function(pillar_weights) {
  stopifnot(setequal(names(pillar_weights), pillars), 
            abs(sum(pillar_weights) - 100) < 1e-9)
  criterion_weights <- unname(pillar_weights[criteria$pillar]) * criteria$share_in_pillar
  by_criterion <- sweep(criterion_scores, 2, criterion_weights, "*")
  by_pillar <- sapply(pillars, function(p) rowSums(by_criterion[, criteria$pillar == p, 
                                                                drop = FALSE]))
  list(pillar_weights = pillar_weights, criterion_weights = criterion_weights,
       by_criterion = by_criterion, by_pillar = by_pillar, total = rowSums(by_criterion))
}

fmt_points <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)

# ----------------------- 4. Tables for one scenario -------------------------
# tie_tolerance_points: models within this many points of the leader are reported as not separable.

build_scenario_tables <- function(weight_performance, weight_robustness, 
                                  weight_explainability,
                                  scenario_name, tie_tolerance_points = 2) {
  points <- compute_points(c(Performance = weight_performance, 
                             Robustness = weight_robustness,
                             Explainability = weight_explainability))
  display_order  <- order(-points$total)
  rank_by_points <- rank(-points$total, ties.method = "min")
  within_tolerance <- points$total >= max(points$total) - tie_tolerance_points

  pillar_table_data <- data.frame(Model = model_names[display_order], check.names = FALSE)
  for (p in pillars) {
    pillar_table_data[[sprintf("%s (%g)", p, points$pillar_weights[[p]])]] <-
      fmt_points(points$by_pillar[display_order, p])
  }
  pillar_table_data[["Total (100)"]] <- fmt_points(points$total[display_order])
  pillar_table_data[["Rank"]] <- rank_by_points[display_order]
  pillar_table_data[["Within tolerance of top"]] <- ifelse(within_tolerance[display_order], 
                                                           "Yes", "No")

  criterion_table_data <- data.frame(Model = model_names[display_order], check.names = FALSE)
  for (j in seq_len(nrow(criteria))) {
    criterion_table_data[[sprintf("%s (%s)", 
                                  criteria$criterion[j], 
                                  fmt_points(points$criterion_weights[j]))]] <-
      fmt_points(points$by_criterion[display_order, j])
  }
  criterion_table_data[["Total (100)"]] <- fmt_points(points$total[display_order])

  list(
    pillars  = themed_table(pillar_table_data,
                            caption = paste0(scenario_name, 
                                             ": pillar summary (points out of 100)"),
                            align = paste0("l", strrep("r", 
                                                       ncol(pillar_table_data) - 1))),
    criteria = themed_table(criterion_table_data,
                            caption = paste0(scenario_name, 
                                             ": points by criterion (maximum in brackets)"),
                            align = paste0("l", strrep("r", 
                                                       ncol(criterion_table_data) - 1))),
    points   = points
  )
}

# --------- 5. Checks on what the weights actually do -----------------
# Spread of points across models for each pillar: a pillar whose models score alike cannot change the
# ranking, whatever its nominal weight.
effective_weights <- function(points) {
  spread <- apply(points$by_pillar, 2, function(x) max(x) - min(x))
  data.frame(Pillar = names(spread),
             `Nominal weight` = points$pillar_weights[names(spread)],
             `Spread of points across models` = fmt_points(spread),
             `Effective share (%)` = fmt_points(100 * spread / sum(spread)),
             check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
}

# Share of random pillar weightings (uniform over all weights summing to 100) in which each model ranks first
share_ranked_first <- function(n_draws = 10000, seed = 2034) {
  set.seed(seed)
  w <- matrix(rexp(n_draws * length(pillars)), ncol = length(pillars))
  w <- 100 * w / rowSums(w)
  totals  <- pillar_scores_01 %*% t(w)  # models x draws
  winners <- factor(rownames(pillar_scores_01)[apply(totals, 2, which.max)],
                    levels = rownames(pillar_scores_01))
  data.frame(Model = model_names,
             `Share of weightings ranked first (%)` = fmt_points(100 * as.numeric(table(winners)) / n_draws),
             check.names = FALSE)
}
```

```{r accuracy-led-pricing, echo=FALSE}
scenario_accuracy_led <- build_scenario_tables(weight_performance = 60, 
                                               weight_robustness = 20,
                                               weight_explainability = 20,
                                               scenario_name = "Accuracy-led pricing")
scenario_accuracy_led$pillars
scenario_accuracy_led$criteria

themed_table(effective_weights(scenario_accuracy_led$points), 
             caption = "Nominal and effective weights")
themed_table(share_ranked_first(), caption = "Rank-first share across random weightings")
```

In a similar way, governance-led pricing reverses the weights assigned, to prioritise robustness and explainability over performance.

```{r governance-pricing, echo=FALSE}
scenario_governance_led <- build_scenario_tables(weight_performance = 20, 
                                                 weight_robustness = 60,
                                                 weight_explainability = 20,
                                                 scenario_name = "Governance-led pricing")
scenario_governance_led$pillars
scenario_governance_led$criteria

themed_table(effective_weights(scenario_governance_led$points), 
             caption = "Nominal and effective weights")
themed_table(share_ranked_first(), caption = "Rank-first share across random weightings")
```

The balanced approach evens out the weights between the three criteria. The models rank as follows:

```{r balanced-pricing, echo=FALSE}
scenario_balanced_led <- build_scenario_tables(weight_performance = 34, 
                                                 weight_robustness = 33,
                                                 weight_explainability = 33,
                                                 scenario_name = "Balanced pricing")
scenario_balanced_led$pillars
scenario_balanced_led$criteria

themed_table(effective_weights(scenario_balanced_led$points), 
             caption = "Nominal and effective weights")
themed_table(share_ranked_first(), caption = "Rank-first share across random weightings")
```
